utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I hope that everybody had a restful recess. Before we proceed with the witness, I would like to deal with one scheduling matter and one matter related to an exhibit, and issue two oral rulings. First, the Chamber is in receipt of a motion filed by Mr. Karadzic on 10th of August to suspend the trial proceedings for a period of three weeks so that he can review certain material disclosed to him by the Prosecution. The Chamber will issue its decision on this motion shortly. However, we have decided to proceed with hearing the evidence of Mr. Mole, Mr. Higgs, and Mr. Blaszczyk, as well as to complete the cross-examination of Mr. Suljevic, as we do not consider these witnesses to be affected by the issues raised in the motion. In other words, the examination and cross-examination of these witnesses can be conducted without any prejudice to the accused from having not yet completed his review of the video and audio files that are subject of the motion. The Chamber will issue its decision on the motion tomorrow or Thursday, which will address whether an adjournment of any period is merited following the completion of evidence of these witnesses. Having said that, can we ask what arrangements have been made to bring Mr. Suljevic back to the court to complete his testimony, and when that will occur. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd have to double-check on that. My recollection, however, was that his availability was as of the 25th. I can't say at this moment whether a fixed date has been arranged in light of the rest of the schedule, so it's a matter of -- it's a matter of whether or not an obvious opening occurs that wouldn't otherwise have disrupted the schedule. But I'll get an answer to the Court this morning so you'll be aware of what the options are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher would kindly bring a headphone for Judge Lattanzi. I note, in addition, that as for the scheduling issue, there's a space available in this courtroom on Friday afternoon of this week, i.e., Friday, the 20th August. So we shall sit from 9.00 to 2.30, as usual. The next agenda concerns an exhibit which was admitted as Exhibit P1219, under seal, on the basis of Ms. Sutherland's submission that it is a medical record of a protected witness in this case. And the Chamber checked that the witness is not the one who is protected in this case, so if the Prosecution could clarify as soon as possible so that we can sort it out. Next, I will give the Chamber's ruling on two of the pending motions. On 28th of July, 2010, Mr. Karadzic requested the presence of the Defence expert Dr. Zorica Subotic in the courtroom during the testimony of three Prosecution witnesses. The Prosecution did not oppose this request. In light of the anticipated technical nature of these witnesses' testimony, we will grant the request to have Dr. Subotic present in the courtroom during that testimony. The Chamber will now issue its decision on the Prosecution's request for leave to call John Hamel as partial 92 ter witness and notification of submission of written evidence, which was filed on 26th of July, 2010. Following the Prosecution's earlier request that, inter alia, the evidence of John Hamel be admitted into evidence in this case pursuant to Rule 92 bis, the Chamber had determined that the witness should come for cross-examination, and, thus, the provisions of Rule 92 ter would apply. In its latest request, the Prosecution notes that it has now identified a number of documents which relate directly to John Hamel's evidence, and it seeks to call the witness as a partial Rule 92 ter witness in order to tender those additional documents through him. The accused filed his response on 3rd of August, stating he has no objection to the Prosecution's request. The Chamber has considered the arguments advanced by the Prosecution in support of its request, the accused's position, and the place of John Hamel on the Prosecution's list of witnesses. The Chamber is satisfied that it is in the interest of justice to grant the request, and John Hamel will appear as a partial Rule 92 ter witness as provided for in the Prosecution's notification for that witness. Finally, I should note for the record the Chamber advised the parties yesterday that applying the criteria it has previously set out to determine an appropriate time for Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination of each witness brought by the Prosecution, it considers that a period of three hours should be sufficient for the cross-examination of Richard Mole. Unless there's on the procedural matters to be raised by the parties, please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, as we have discussed, your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing, so let me first address some preliminary formalities associated with that submission. You have previously provided statements to the Office of the Prosecutor in September 1997 and April 2002?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And you testified in the case of Stanislav Galic on the 3rd and the 7th of June and the 2nd to the 4th of July, 2002?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Did you meet with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor earlier this year and prepare a statement that amalgamated your prior evidence, which you then signed on the 7th of May, 2010?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yeah, I've had that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And I believe there is one amendment that you wish to make to that statement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we can 65 ter 90180, please. And if we can move to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And at paragraph 12, you are discussing observation posts, and you state: "... there were approximately seven manned observation posts on each side." Now, Colonel Mole, after looking at your end-of-month reports, can you confirm that you wish to change this to read: "With respect to monitoring of weapons, there were 14 observation posts. At the end of October, 1992, 10 were on the Lima side and 4 on the Papa side. By the end of November 1992, there were 11 on the Lima side and 3 on the Papa side, and this remained the case until my departure"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: With that clarification, can you confirm that the statement is accurate and that if you were asked the same questions on the same topics today, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, in those circumstances, I tender 65 ter 90180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'll now read a brief summary of the evidence contained in that statement. Lieutenant-Colonel Richard Mole served in the British Military for 23 years prior to his arrival in Sarajevo. From 16 September to 26th December, 1992, he was the senior military observer for the United Nations Military Observers in Sarajevo, commonly referred to as UNMOs. In this position, he was in charge of approximately 60 observers positioned on both sides of the confrontation lines, who were mandated to, among other things, monitor and report on heavy weapons activity. Colonel Mole recalls that there was not a single day of his tour in Sarajevo that there were no shell impacts in the city. He observed shelling and immense damage from shelling in areas of the city away from the confrontation lines. Random shelling made the whole city an extremely dangerous place to live in. UNMO's estimated that during this period 14 to 15 civilian people died per day as a result of shelling or sniping. Colonel Mole sought explanations from Sarajevo Romanija Corps commanders for their firing into the city. On one occasion, he was told by a commander, who was firing a mortar round, that he was "warming the barrels." On another, that the three rounds that had just been fired were one for each finger of the Serb salute. Colonel Mole frequently met with SRK Commander General Galic and protested the indiscriminate shelling. On a number of occasions during these meetings, General Galic threatened to shell Sarajevo city if events elsewhere did not transpire in the Bosnian Serbs' favour. For example, on one occasion General Galic said that if fire from Mount Igman onto the headquarters at Lukavica did not cease, there would be reciprocal fire onto the city of Sarajevo. Colonel Mole came to the view that the Bosnian Serb strategy around Sarajevo was a, quote, "policy of containment" such that they would apply pressure to the city in order to achieve their aims elsewhere. That concludes the summary. I will now briefly clarify with Colonel Mole a few aspects of the evidence in his statement. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 17010, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, the Chamber has heard some evidence concerning reports of UNMOs in Sarajevo. I'd now like to clarify with you some aspects of the UNMO reporting process that you describe at paragraphs 24 to 29 of your statement. In paragraph 24, you describe a standardised report that was used by observers to record their observations. Is the document that you see on the screen in front of you that type of report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This report comes from an observation post. How were the observation posts or the locations of the observation posts determined?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: To a degree, I inherited the locations of both observation posts and weapon monitoring teams. At this stage, I think it's important to differentiate between the two. On the Lima side, that is, those locations outside of the city, the weapon monitoring was the major role of the UN military observers, for that was where the heavy weapons were located and was the task that I'd inherited, which had originated from the airport agreement earlier in 1992, before I assumed command in Sarajevo. Within the city, we had a similar function. There was collection of heavy weapons, but it wasn't such a significant task by virtue of there being less heavy weapons on the Presidency side than to the Serb side. That leads me now into answering your question which relates to the document I have in front of me. It's what we call an increp. It's an incident report. Both sides would have used these, and when I say "both sides," I mean both on Lima side, that is, Serb side, and on Papa side, that is, Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, let me ask you about some of the terms and acronyms that are used in this report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You've described this as an increp. What did the term "increp" mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That's "incident report."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And we see at the top of the page the term "Papa 5" or "P 5." And what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That would relate to the location from whence this report was sourced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, if we look down at the columns and to the left-hand side, the first column is entitled "Serial." What's recorded here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: What you see under that column is "P5" or "Papa 5," which indicates the location, and then after that a serial number which is sequential for any particular 24-hour period, which would start at 1.00 until the end of that 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we move from left to right on this chart, we see there's the time, the date, and the fourth column is entitled "Activity Details." What's recorded here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Here we have the time of each of the incidents recorded on the first paragraph or serial, the period of that incident given in the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And in the first row, we see terms "RT/MR," et cetera. What did those terms stand for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes. Under "Activity Details," which is para 4, would be the detail of the event, and this would relate to the type of weapons used and what had been observed, the number of strikes, and any other pertinent information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The next column across, para 5, entitled "Source of Information," and in each and every row we see the term "UNMO Seen" written. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: We could, if we wished to, take our source of information from other sides' UN military observers, but I always asked observers to be the prime source of information, as that was the source of information that was the most trustworthy. So most of the entries there would be UN military observer seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If that's the case and the predominant source, as you've stated, was UNMOs personally observing the action, can you be confident that on any given day in Sarajevo, every round of heavy weapons activity would be recorded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: You couldn't say that every round -- that ever heavy weapons activity was recorded, for the number of locations, observation locations, was limited by the number of officers I had available. But we tried to ensure that the Papa locations were in such places as to cover the majority of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And the final column is entitled "Remarks." We see the names of places as well as four-digit numbers. What did those numbers indicate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes. The incident would presumably have a source or a result of the source, and that was put into that column, and a grid reference was appended to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: What would happen to these reports from the observation posts once they were completed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: You can see that there is considerable detail. Movement within the city was restricted, so at the top of the form which you've got displayed you have paragraphs 1 through to 6, and that allowed the locations to radio through a summary of the events of the day to myself at my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And what would you do with that information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That information would be assimilated and submitted then to my line commander, the chief military observer, who was then located in Zagreb. I would also ensure that copies were passed to my sector commander, who was General Razek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I can tender the document on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we can hear something more about the page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Certainly. If we turn to page 2, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, what do we see indicated on the second page of this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: In the normal run of events, one would expect the first page that we had viewed to be sufficient for task. However, this was during an exceptional period where we had to turn over the page. And it was during the assault on Otes, and Papa 5 was located in such a position it was able to watch the whole event. And the strike rate of heavy artillery within the concentrated area of Otes was unbelievable, and I think that page describes it. It's a series of five rounds at a time over the period that daylight permitted that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we go back to page 1. Colonel Mole, if you could explain the calculation which is done at the right side of this document. 1087, plus 12, plus 10. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you must remember that, sir, I wasn't actually at Papa 5 throughout the engagement, although I was there for a considerable time. What the officers were trying to do was to record all the heavy weapon strikes within a concentrated area over a period of a few days. This, I accept, is just one day. What they were attempting to do was to rationalise the irrational. That's just a total which was summarised to pass on, presumably, to myself that day for the amount of rounds that were landing on Otes at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I note also a name there. It says "From P5, the best regards is" -- I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that for you, should you wish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This particular document, or a copy of it, was given to me as a gift by my officers at Papa 5. So what you see at the top there, which is epitomised by the comment "Best regards" was passed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hayden, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can ask for 65 ter 17026, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, you described the manner in which you assimilated the information and would send that up to Zagreb. Is this the type of assimilation that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, so that's the form that I would use to submit the dates that we've discussed so far when I had collated it from all locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This is a two-page document. Would you typically author this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, though I should add a caveat. I had an operations room and I had an operations staff. I had a deputy senior military observer who ran that operations room for me, and that staff and that deputy would, of course, do the staff work required of me. But for as long as I have signed that report, I would have been party to its creation and obviously take responsibility for its submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The information we see recorded here, would that reflect information from observation posts recorded on the same day or was there a time lag?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: There would be, of course, a small time lag. It was very dependent upon the activity within the city to permit the detailed reports to be submitted to me. But as I've already indicated, the daily reports could, by use of the serial numbers, be submitted to me on the radio. So the outline information which I was able to collate for all the observation points was available to me relatively quickly at the end of a 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I tender that document into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1428, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I would ask for 65 ter 10865, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, you mention in your statement that compilation reports were produced at the end of each of the three months you were in Sarajevo. Is the document on the screen in front of you one such report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just, firstly, I note that the SMO there is listed as Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler. Can you explain why his name appears and not yours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Indeed. The latter part of December was the time I finished my tour, and Colonel Cutler took over for me. So at the end of the month, he will have signed the report. Much of the content of the report, of course, would have been mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2, please. If we look down at the 4th of December entry, which is the final paragraph, Colonel Mole, does this reflect the information in the daily situation report that was just on our screens a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I think it probably answers the question I was posed relating to the numerics of the first sheet. But I think it might be helpful at this stage if I might just elaborate that the daily reports that I submitted, which we've already seen prior to this, the monthly report, were created not just by the input from observation points, weapons sites, but they were inclusive of information that I gathered myself from multiple agencies, the other battalions within the UNPROFOR protected area, which was Sarajevo, the three battalions, UNHCR, Red Cross. Many other agencies would go to contribute towards the report I created daily, and that would have an effect, obviously, upon this report which we now have in front of us, so that's why the detail here goes well beyond what we saw from the very first report from observation points.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, in a number of daily entries we see a discrepancy between the number of incoming rounds impacting into the city, or the Papa or Presidency side, and the number of outgoing rounds recorded on the Lima side, or the Bosnian Serb side. For example, if we look at this entry for 4 December, we see that there were 1.480 rounds incoming to Presidency side, and 30 rounds -- I apologise, and 203 outgoing rounds recorded from the Bosnian Serb side. How do you explain such discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: As I intimated initially, I inherited the result of the airport agreement which was finalised before I arrived in Sarajevo. That gave me a task to me of monitoring heavy weapons on both sides, but that is to assume that all the heavy weapons on both sides had been gathered into the weapon monitoring sites that we've already discussed, with the numbers of locations of observation points and weapon monitoring teams on both sides which we were talking about when we first started the discussion. Now, it's clear that not all heavy weapons were either directly or indirectly observed by UN personnel, and certainly not by the only 60 officers that I had available to me for both sides. So there were logistic limitations as well as agreement limitations as to how many weapons were monitored, and I hope, therefore, you see that the difference between the rounds you've identified coming in and observed going out will vary by virtue of the number of weapons that we were monitoring. There were significant numbers of weapons which we didn't monitor, were not party to the agreement, and also, of course, were brought into the region for a specific military objective. The Otes experience was one such military activity. Weapons were brought in from elsewhere into the region for that operation. I hope that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we can turn to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, we also see that discrepancy going the other way; that is, the number of outgoing rounds from the Presidency side and the number of incoming on the Serb side. For example, if we look here at 6 December, we see that there were 136 rounds incoming to the Serb side, but only 12 recorded outgoing from the Presidency positions. Is the explanation the same here or are there additional factors at play?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It's a very similar explanation, but one which popular understanding of the situation in Sarajevo does not seem to encompass. If I might explain. The numbers of heavy weapons within the Presidency side within the city were extremely limited, which I think I've explained; hence, the major function of the UN Military Observers was not so much weapon monitoring, but observing. However, available to the Presidency side were significant heavy weapons, which we had no observation upon, outside Sarajevo and beyond the front-line which the Serbs had between them and the Presidency side. I'll give, by example, Mount Igman, where significant weapons on the Presidency side were brought to bear upon Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I tender the document in front of us into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1429, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I would ask Mr. Registrar for 65 ter 10863, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, did you provide a map to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And is this the map before you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who drew the lines we see and what they depict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I created the map. When I took over the task of senior military observer, I had very little in the way of a hand-over take-over in a formal fashion. I didn't even know where the front-lines were, so I made it my business to find those front-lines. I went both within and outside the city, right the way 'round the 64-kilometre circumference, which is the near complete circle you see at the top of that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, in the daily and monthly reports we've looked at a moment ago, we frequently see phrases such as "indiscriminate shelling of city" or "shelling widely dispersed throughout the city." I'd like to briefly explore with you what those phrases mean. First, and perhaps by reference to the map, what did you consider to be the city?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Within the near complete circle at the top of the map was what we considered the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Was the -- when you used the phrase "the city," did it encompass the areas proximate to the confrontation line or was it distinct from that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. The front-line was as I have drawn on the map, but, of course, the area of conflict would be a certain depth either side of that line. There's nothing definitive about this particular sort of warfare. So when we talk about the city, I talk about any built-up area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: What did you mean by the term "indiscriminate shelling" or "widely dispersed shelling"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I think we have to perhaps consider, in answering that question, what the aims or objectives might be of those that use heavy weapons. Most heavy weapons are indirect-fire weapons. By virtue of them being indirect-fire weapons, their accuracy is not all that one might expect. The solution to that lack of accuracy, when you're using heavy weapons, is to have a specific fire mission where you bring to bear intense artillery fire in a concentrated area to achieve a specific aim. If you do not perceive a specific aim, if the fire that is coming in is not concentrated, one immediately asks the question: What is its purpose? If one thinks of a command structure of the units that are using that fire, as a commander I would want to know how much ammunition I have and how it is used. That is why I would be a commander. So I'd want to know every round that was fired and for what purpose, for, after all, as a commander I command those units. So having observed fire from those able to provide it, when you see the result of that activity, you would expect a pattern. If a pattern which I've described as a fire mission was not evident, then I would call that indiscriminate fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And just to clarify, Colonel Mole, what type of observations would be made on a day in which the report would state there was indiscriminate or widely-dispersed shelling?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: To answer that question, I think it's very important to understand the background noise and intensity in a city that was under siege for such a long period. The noise never ceased, it was persistent, and so we would put down, on a situation report for the end of a day, that it had been a quiet day if about 100 rounds had landed in the city. A fairly active day would be in the 400 to 500 mark. An extremely active day would be 600 upwards. So an average day, perhaps in answer to your question, would be about 100 rounds, but that's high explosive. And I haven't even started to talk about direct-fire weapons, such as small arms, infantry weapons, which are mortars -- include mortars as an indirect-fire weapon, heavy mortars, heavy machine-guns, anti-aircraft fire used in a direct-fire mode. And that is the background noise that a city made every day, so to concentrate purely on the 100 rounds high explosive coming in from indirect-fire weapons is to trivialise life in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, from your military experience and your experience in Sarajevo, what type of visual damage would you expect a heavy weapon -- a high-calibre heavy weapon shell to inflict on, for example, a multi-storey concrete building, a single shell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I think there is a popular misconception that a high explosive round such as you describe of about the calibre 155 would make the same sort of damage as what we would loosely call a bomb, i.e., a bomb from an aircraft. It is totally different. Of course, the significance if you're within the proximity of such a high explosive round detonating is immense, but surprisingly the damage that is left isn't necessarily as extensive as one might expect. Perhaps the easiest way to express this would be: If you took a heavy mortar round, which would be at the lower end of the weapon size that you have asked me to answer the question on, if it landed on tarmac there would be a mark on the ground where the shrapnel obviously in the close proximity to the explosion had marked the ground, but there would be little other damage. So you can transpose that picture to maybe the top of a block of flats. Should a 155 round drop vertically on to it, yes, it would do damage on the immediate vicinity of its strike, and, of course, it would certainly do damage to people should they be there, if they were in the direct vicinity of the explosion. But the point is that the building, itself, would still stand and it would not look as if it had been that badly damaged. Can I make another example, if I may. There was film which I've seen of before I arrived in Sarajevo, of the Parliament building being directly attacked by a combination of heavy machine-gun rounds and direct-fire anti-aircraft weapons. It was pounded for hours, yet when I went to Sarajevo, the building was still there. Of course, it was burnt out. Of course, anybody who had been living or trying to work in that environment during the attack would have been killed. But it puts balance on the sort of damage that one saw as one went 'round the city. This sort of damage, the limited damage belies the intensity of high-explosive detonation that occurred in Sarajevo. So to those who hadn't experienced it, they may be surprised that the city survived at all. But I hope that explanation gives you some indication of the balance between the numbers of rounds that came into the city throughout the siege and the residual buildings within the city and what they looked like at the end of the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can tender the map on the screen in front of us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1430, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, you were in Sarajevo from September until December 1992. Can you briefly describe to the Chamber what it was like living in that environment for three months?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Really, I have to develop what I've already tried to express in terms of the type of rounds, the type of persistent, constant small arms right through the range of weapons to high-explosive indirect-fire weapons. It was a constant threat. Now, one would expect during a war, which this was, that the conflict would be concentrated around the front-line. One would expect that. So the next expectation would be that one should, assuming one is careful with collateral damage, be able to move around the city relatively freely. You'll excuse me, but there's a perverse logic in that which I'm trying to explain that you can move 'round a city during a war, but now I'm going to add the caveats. War isn't exact, it's not a science. It's not even an art. Collateral damage is huge. With collateral damage, we can express any opinion or support any of our own particular observations by using collateral damage as the excuse. But you would still expect, as my task was, to move 'round the city freely and, indeed, to go across the front-lines virtually every day. You would expect to do some of those activities and have areas of concern. So when I went to the airport, I would expect a certain stress and a certain pressure because I'm going across a front-line. Believe me, the pressure was there, direct and indirect, because I couldn't start to express to you the number of times where direct fire was directed at not just me, personally, but the vehicle I was in and other UN soldiers. But I still put the caveat that I would expect that. I was moving around in a war and I'm going across a front-line. It's a very abnormal situation to be in. But I would still expect that within the city, I would have a relative safety because it isn't an area of direct conflict. Now, because within the city there is a military structure, there will be, within that city, quite clearly, military objectives. But I've already described to you if I was on one side or the other, if I want to target a military objective, how I would do it. One would locate it and would put down a fire mission, which is a concentrated fire mission, to resolve my problem. But that wasn't the way that the city happened. Wherever you went, whatever you did, you were subject to this incessant fear and concern that that journey you were on was going to complete. If it was like that for me, then within the highly populated areas of the city, where people had no choice, where they had to live their lives - they didn't have vehicles like I did - that fear was immense and protracted. We, as visitors there, experienced it for a relatively short time. I hope that starts to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President. At this stage, I would tender the remaining documents from the 92 ter statement. There's just two points to note there, from a housekeeping point of view. The first is that one of the exhibits referred to in that 92 ter statement is already in evidence, 65 ter 10670 is P1259, and the second is that 65 ter 22801, which is a map that identifies the observation posts of the UNMOs, was not on the Prosecution's original 65 ter list. We did seek leave to add it in the 92 ter notification filed in May this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that request is granted. And then you said that 65 ter 10670 has been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Then unless there's any objection, all the other associated exhibits will be admitted, and the exhibit numbers will be given in due course by the Registrar. Thank you, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to cross-examine Colonel Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all. Welcome back from your vacations. I hope the Chamber will reconsider the question of time for cross-examination, in view of the developments involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Mole. May I express my gratitude to you for having met up with the Defence yesterday as well. I see today that my learned friend on the other side brought things back to his own line during his questioning, which is only to be commended. Let us go back to the question of Otes. It's not in chronological order, but it may be useful. In your amalgamated statement, in paragraph 35 you said: [In English] "There in his --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, do you like to have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The physical statement as opposed to on the screen? Yeah. I have one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out in English because I'm quoting the statement of Colonel Mole: [In English] "Indirectly, the Serbs practiced containment, maintaining the status quo in Sarajevo and not trying to significantly alter the position of the front-lines." [Interpretation] Is that right? Is that in paragraph 35 of your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I think the numbering on my statement might be different. I'm not sure that I've got para 35. Wait a minute. I have it. What you read in the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll do my best to put as many yes/no questions as possible. Is this legitimate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Sorry, you're asking me if that's legitimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean, is that kind of military position to be taken by the Serbian side, is that legitimate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Many of the questions which sound relatively simple, which may demand a yes/no answer within this environment, require much more detail to answer satisfactorily. So I would like to add that as a rider to answering your questions, but I will be as brief as possible. So in this instance, it's a general policy upon which I am describing there over the whole long-term siege of Sarajevo. It does not, therefore, take into account tactical variations, which is what I would describe Otes as, as opposed to strategic objective, which is what I would describe the siege of Sarajevo as, within the context of Bosnia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in P14428 [as interpreted] that has just been admitted, that's your memo dated, well, from 1992, in paragraph 15 you concluded that the Serb offensive was: [In English] " ... likely response to perceived observation by Muslims to connect Butmir to Otes and break the siege --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, could you wait until the witness and the Chamber can see the para 15 you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that there are only seven paras in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think Dr. Karadzic is actually referring to one of the amalgamated exhibits that is -- or one of the associated exhibits that has not yet received a number. It's actually 65 ter 17030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. That is actually correct. Yes, we have number 15 here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [In English] Otes was: "... likely response to perceived operation by Muslims to connect Butmir to Otes and break the siege. Muslims had made exploratory moves in the weeks before." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the correct document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be right. Perhaps it's just another paragraph, but I think it's the right document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read it from the screen: [In English] "... the pocket the Serbs find themselves in the west of the city, between the Croats (north-west-south-west) and Presidency (south), Igman, and the loss of access east (airport). Without going into unnecessary detail, the intention of the operation was to connect Butmir to Otes and squeeze the pocket from Zuc. Exploratory moves had been made by the Presidency out of Otes a matter of weeks before."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these military operations, as it were, were they legitimate, these operations carried out by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I perceive these movements and this activity to be military, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that from Otes, there were constant attacks against the Serb part of Ilidza? Your colleagues who testified here, UN officers, confirmed that; namely, that from Otes, there was permanent pressure exerted against the Serb part of Ilidza and attacks were carried out as well.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to ask for 1D2222 in e-court, please. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, paragraph 7: [In English] "According to the UN source, the Serbs could also be trying to head off an expected Bosnian offensive aimed at breaking the siege of Sarajevo. "A total of 15.000 Croats and Muslim troops are said to have massed south-west of Sarajevo and are reported to be equipped with heavy weaponry."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for this report of Agence France-Presse, does that respond to the reports that you sent and to your knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Of the two paragraphs from this source, which until yesterday I had not seen, the first of the two paragraphs to which you refer, the one stating "according to the UN source, the Serbs could also be trying to head off," that paragraph relates quite accurately with the assessment that I made and we already discussed. At this stage, I think it's important to note that I wasn't the UN source, and I don't know who it was. As for the second paragraph about the assumption of the Croat/Muslim troops south-west of Sarajevo, we had no evidence of that. That's not to say it wasn't true, but we had no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, you said that you also used information that you received from other sources, not only from your own observers, that is to say, agencies, and I assume that France Presse is an agency that one would respect and that you would respect. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Until yesterday, I'd never heard of them. They certainly weren't represented at any of the meetings I went to in Sarajevo. Some agencies did appear at our briefing sessions that the sector commander held every day. Those agencies would, by example, be UNHCR, Red Cross, and similar, but it never, ever included elements of the press. The only press that I had direct dealings with were a small team of BBC reporters who lived alongside us at the PTT building. I've also stated in my various submissions that not always does the press reflect a balanced affair nor an understanding view of the circumstance that I experienced in Sarajevo. I'm afraid that's a long answer to a simple question about this particular submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to the media, because, indeed, you had observed that there was a discrepancy between the map and the actual terrain, or, rather, in terms of their own reporting. Colonel, this is what I would be interested in: When you said that you included UNHCR reports and those from other agencies, did you include this information on the basis of contacts you had with them, or their reports, or what was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: If I may explain again that daily we had a joint briefing in the PTT building, which was our sector headquarters. Now, I think it important to understand that although I passed information to my sector headquarters, my line of command was directly to the chief military observer in Zagreb, whose direct line of command above him was the UNPROFOR commander. That's the significance of UN military observers, that they have a direct line of command to the UN commander. That command structure was in evidence in Sarajevo, so that I worked with the sector commander, but he was not my commander. Hence, I was at those briefings as a contributor and also to assimilate such information as I could from the agencies that you talk of. Like myself, I was amongst others who were reporting to and listening at what the sector had to say in support of that sector. I, therefore, if I heard a report at such a meeting from a recognised attendant such as a UNHCR representative, I would take those views to be the truth from the perception of the person expressing them, much as I would expect my own views, my own assessments, both humanitarian and military, to be taken seriously by the sector commander when I submitted them. I say again it does not include the press. This was not a briefing to the public. This was a military sector planning meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is very useful. These exhaustive answers of yours are very useful, but they are restricting my own time for cross-examination, so I'm hoping for somewhat shorter answers. Let us try to spell this out in very specific terms. There were no media present at these briefings. It was only the military observers, the UNHCR, and the International Red Cross, and who else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The sector representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR, you mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, I did list them as well, but it doesn't seem to have been interpreted. All right. Was there anyone else there, in addition to the UNHCR, the Red Cross? Was it the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It was, but the gentleman concerned was only there for about two weeks and then he absconded with the money which he had been given to do his job, so his contribution was not too significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any contact with journalists from Sky News?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We had a witness here from Sky News, and he said that he informed UNPROFOR and that UNPROFOR informed him. So this exchange of information was mutual. Did any of your co-workers or associates maintain contact with Sky News, or the BBC, for that matter? Who did you co-operate with and who did you exchange information with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: With the media, I exchanged or co-operated not at all. It was not my job to assist them in any fashion, and I instructed my officers not to talk to the press. So there was no dialogue with them, because it didn't fall within the duty of a UN military observer to discuss anything with the press. If anything was to be discussed with the press, then it would be me that did the discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, we'll have a break for 20 minutes, and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, after our interview and after reviewing your statements and reports, I also reviewed the reports of the news agency Srna, S-r-n-a, and all your reports are, indeed, confirmed by agency reports. And if we had time, I would tender them into evidence, but I believe I will eventually tender them as part of a Bar table motion. Now I would like to go back to Otes, and I would like to call for 65 ter 106865 [as interpreted]. I believe it has been admitted today as 1429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, did you want to tender that AFP report into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D534, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 10865. If I'm right, it has been admitted today as P1429. It's a monthly report in which you say, and I believe that's on the next page -- the date is 4 December --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Extremely high level of activity today with 1480 rounds incoming to Presidency side and 30 rounds to Serb side. Total round recording outgoing from Serb positions, 203; Presidency, 26. Majority of shelling in west of city, particularly in area of Otes. Presidency corps commander has announced on TV that Otes is about to fall and has requested UNPROFOR assistance to evacuate women" -- woman -- women, probably, "women and children. Received unconfirmed reports that Presidency force launched infantry attack on broad front in the south-west of city, likely to relieve pressure on Otes." [Interpretation] First of all, do you recall this report, and were women and children, indeed, evacuated? Is everything in this paragraph correct, as far as these events is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, we discussed a bit the unity -- the unified character of the war. Was it legitimate for the Muslims, in this case, to attack us to relieve pressure on Otes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It seems as if it was an acceptable response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to your amalgamated statement, paragraphs 84 and 85. In these paragraphs - I don't know if we can get them on the screen, but I can summarise them - you explained that Muslims achieved certain progress on another front-line facing Zuc, and the Serb artillery was legitimately trained at Otes and Zuc, but at the same time persistent shelling continued on all sections of the city. I'd like to know if that is correct, and, if so, what percentage of the rounds were directed at Zuc and at Otes, in view of the term you used earlier, "indiscriminate shelling"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Taking your question as two parts, I see you ask "but at the same time, persistent shelling continued on all sections of the city. I'd like to know if that is correct." My answer to that is, yes, that is correct. You then say: "If so, what percentage of the rounds were directed at Zuc and at Otes, in view of the term you used earlier, 'indiscriminate shelling.'" If we accept that what occurred at Zuc and Otes was a military action for tactical advantage, it's difficult to put a percentage, but it would be a low percentage of 10, 15 per cent, but it's a very vague guess. My point in making this statement is there was shelling elsewhere in the city that was not pertinent to the two military operations to which you refer correctly at Zuc and at Otes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I now call 1D2227 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting: Would you agree that in addition to these two operations by the Muslims directed at Zuc and the Serbian counter-offensive directed at Otes -- let us first get one thing clear. Do you agree that the Serbian action against Otes was a counter-offensive, and do you know about the preceding constant attacks on Ilidza directed from Otes? It's in your reports.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Can we clarify what, in this context, "counter-offensive" means? To me, as a soldier, a counter-offensive would be a response to a very specific series of actions. I, therefore, understand your use of it in this context as a response to a persistent that the Serbs perceived they had from Otes, and, therefore, I understand the tactical response. I wouldn't particularly call that a counter-offensive, but I understand the military logic for the offence on Otes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This seems to be 2221, and we need 2227. I'm sorry, we need 2221, actually. Thank you for this answer. We will go back to certain documents that relate to what you've just said; long-term Muslim actions sourced at Otes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here we have a report from the France Presse agency, and I hope the French will not hold it against me that you are not familiar with this news agency. It is a well-respected agency where I come from. Let us see what they say about the 2nd of December: [In English] "The airport sector was calm overnight after Tuesday's confrontation between Muslim-Croat defenders of the city and Bosnian Serb attackers, in which hospital sources said 40 of 56 injured were fighters." [Interpretation] Let us now see where is the part that mentions Otes. Just a moment. The sixth paragraph: "Today's fighting around the airport started when Bosnian infantry units attacked Serbian forces stationed in the village of Ilidza, which borders the airport. "The Serbs responded with intense artillery fire that shook the entire sector, Commander Barry Frewer, a spokesman of the United Nations troops in Sarajevo, said, Wednesday." [Interpretation] Do you remember -- do you know this gentleman, Barry Frewer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: He wasn't under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he was an UNPROFOR spokesperson, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that in parallel with the fighting for Otes and Zuc, there was fighting in other parts of the city as well? Lower- intensity fighting, perhaps, but it went on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: During the Otes offensive, we noticed no variation in what we would perceive as the normal front-line activities elsewhere in the city. As I have indicated, there was some shelling which came into the city, but I revert to my earlier statement that if that was in response to a particular military action, one would expect that that fire mission would be more concentrated than it was. That is the second reason, I would say, that there was no noticeable or discernible increase in front-line activity, other than that that we've discussed, in the two areas, Zuc and Otes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D535, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call 1D2223.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, this is an AFP report. I don't think you will forget them ever again, after all the use we've made of their reports. Let's see what they put out for the 8th December, after Otes fell into Serb hands: [In English] "Serb forces cut road access to Sarajevo Airport on Tuesday, the day before it was reopened for the UN relief effort, as fighting flared in the Bosnia and Herzegovina capital." [Interpretation] And then it goes on to say: [In English] "Meanwhile, some two or five Serb tanks were reported to be firing from the airport road to Slav Muslim Serb of Dobrinja which lies between the airport and the city. The sounds of shelling were loud and frequent in central Sarajevo, about 10 kilometres from Dobrinja." "Bosnian government forces [realtime transcript read in error "Bosnian Serb"], who were mainly Muslim and Croat, were trying to counter-attack after losing the western suburb of Otes to Serb forces last Friday, reliable military sources said. "They said the Serbs were responding to this, rather than mounting a new attack." Do you agree with this AFP report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: One would expect the overall increase in tension throughout the sector when there has been a significant tactical change. The report sounds very reasonable. Was it greater than the normal or average tension? Yes, I would suggest that that's probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To put it briefly, this is a war going on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: To put it briefly, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 6 of this transcript page should read "Bosnian government forces" instead of "Bosnian Serb forces." It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D536, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get P -- or, rather, 65 ter 17030. We called it a moment ago, or was it 18? No, it's 17030. Yes, that's your report from December 1992, in which you envisaged, and that's paragraph 31: [In English] " ... the Serbs are likely not to take further offensive actions, but maintain status quo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that, indeed, the reality until you left Sarajevo on the 26th of December, 1992, and that would be consistent about your general remarks about the Serb position and the maintenance of the status quo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're asking if the statement made in paragraph 31 is the opinion that I held then and proved to be the case until I left Sarajevo. If that's your question, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's already an exhibit. May I now call 1D1179. I don't think this is the right translation. I'm informed we have a translation. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the date, 30th November, 1400 hours, just before the operation in Otes. I'll read in Serbian: "Enemy activity: "In the course of the day, the enemy opened sniper fire and fired rifle grenades on Lukavica from Dobrinja and Mojmilo. "From the direction of Visoko and Salkanov Han, they opened anti-aircraft machine-gun fire on the positions of the Ilijas Brigade. Our units did not return fire. "The UNPROFOR Co-operation Group was informed of cease-fires. "The situation in the area remains unchanged. "One soldier from the Ilijas Brigade was wounded in the leg." Is this consistent with what you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It's a document which I had not seen before now. If I didn't make specific mention of it in any of my reports, then clearly it wasn't observed by UN military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the fact the Serb side did not respond. There was no activity on their part on the 30th of November. There was considerable activity from Mojmilo, from Dobrinja, and Visoko in Central Bosnia, but the Serbian side did not respond. Do you agree? And we notified the UNPROFOR of the activity of the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I note what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you rule out that possibility or do you allow for the possibility that this is, indeed, so, and this was a strictly-confidential report to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I can't answer the question, since I was not party to the correspondence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now call D203 to remind the colonel about the 1st of December, another report to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, just to see what the circumstances were in the theatre of war. D203. 1D01194, that's what it is, otherwise. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to number 1. I'm going to read it out in Serbian: "The enemy has continued with intense methods of attack on the broad region of Ilidza and Rajlovac during the afternoon hours. The enemy has attacked from the region of Igman and the village of Kovaci with heavy artillery, and with infantry fire from the town of Otes directed at the region of Ilidza. In the direction of Sokolje Distribution Centre, the enemy has carried out an unsuccessful infantry attack, with the support of enemy artillery, on the region of Rajlovac." Then number 2 says: "The unit of the brigade of Ilidza retaliated against the enemy attack with a successful counter-attack, and conquered -- and took the line from Azici to Nedzarici, as well as the center of Otes." Do you agree that if somebody carries out an attack and then the other side defends itself and then does something by way of a counter-attack, that that constitutes a counter-offensive, actually?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That all seems a very reasonable military response.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This has already been admitted, right, so could we now have that other document back? I think it was the first one, P1427. Can we have page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to explain this to us. What does this mean, this in the second line or, rather, the second area? What is it that is enumerated there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: As I explained earlier, the format for reporting the use of heavy weapons for reporting impacts within an area was the form you saw on the front of this particular item. Its design, really, was for areas where a cease-fire existed, and you would, therefore, as observers, note the breaking of cease-fires with a limited number of incidents. Of course, as we know, Sarajevo, although it went through a series of notional cease-fires, never really ceased the combat from either side throughout the period that I was there, so what we look at on this form is an extension of the front of the form, which indicates the impacts in a very small area of the city as a result of a military offensive against Otes. If one's critical, then clearly the form's not sufficient for purpose, but the idea was to give an impression of the intensity of the conflict in that region and to try and give an idea to those who were not in the theatre the sort of conflict that was being observed by the UN military observers and UNPROFOR within the sector at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This number, 1.087, does it pertain to all of this? And if so, how much of it fell on Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: You can see, from that form, that we have "Nedzarici" crossed out. I have no understanding of why it was crossed out. We have another title at the bottom, and we have "Otes/Ilica" at the top. I'm afraid since I didn't construct that particular set of hieroglyphics, any further interpretation from myself would be pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber something about Nedzarici, because you do know about Nedzarici, don't you? Am I right if I say that Nedzarici is a purely Serb settlement of small family houses near the airport?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Nedzarici was an enclave of Serb control within the city. The front-line between the Serbs and the Presidency was extremely close. I have detailed knowledge of Nedzarici by virtue of my inheritance of an observation point there when I arrived in the city, placed by my predecessor. Its location in Nedzarici was of no significance for my task, and the dangers associated with my officers being there were out of all proportion to their usefulness, so I removed that particular location and re-deployed the officers concerned. I had many dealings with the commander on the Serb side, with the commander of Nedzarici, and it was interpretation, probably with Grbavica, one of the classic areas of urban warfare that you could ever expect to see. It was always extremely stressful. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have P1430, please. It's a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: Tell me, would you agree that Nedzarici and Grbavica are Serb urban neighbourhoods within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: You're now asking me if I know, I assume, the ethnic make-up of the inhabitants of those two locations. Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and who controlled these neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I can answer the last part. They were controlled from the Serb side. As to ethnic make-up, it's not a question that one can easily answer as, firstly, an outsider; secondly, because we are, as we have agreed, in a war, so who was where before the war started, I am not party to; and, thirdly, to me, as an UNMO fulfilling my task, ethnicity had no significance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now have a look at this map. I believe it is accurate, in terms of the period that we are dealing with. Do you agree that Ilidza is also part of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: We're now discussing whether Ilidza is part of Sarajevo in a geographical sense. I assume it's a suburb of Sarajevo, would be my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the city of Sarajevo consisted of 10 municipalities and that Ilijas was within it, at the north, and then Vogosca at the north in this map, and then Ilidza, Hadzici, Trnovo, and then Pale, and a few municipalities, five municipalities, in the nucleus of town, in the inner city? Do you agree that the town of Sarajevo -- the city of Sarajevo goes far beyond this inner city, as it were, that is marked here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The civil divisions of the city, again, were of -- not of my understanding before I went to Sarajevo. They weren't of particular relevance to me, in my tour, for me to do as I had to do. If you say that that was the civil division of the city, then I have to bow to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to mark Nedzarici for us here. If you could use that electronic pen so that the Trial Chamber and the participants could confirm their insights as far as Sarajevo is concerned yet again.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you place an N there, or, rather, 1. Let's have Nedzarici as number 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where Aerodromsko Naselje, the airport neighbourhood, is? To the south of this number; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the name of the neighbourhood again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aerodromsko Naselje, the airport neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: No, that's not a name I recall. The name I recall for the neighbourhood relating to the airport would be Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you see here that parts of Dobrinja are controlled by the Serb side; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: If you're suggesting the block to the west of the square 'round Dobrinja, if I can point that out [marks], are you talking of that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We call that Aerodromsko Naselje, the airport neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I understand completely. We would have grouped it all under the "Nedzarici" title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark Otes on this map, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Would you like a figure 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serb part of Ilidza, could you mark that as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the transcript, 1 is Nedzarici, including parts of Dobrinja, or, rather, the Aerodromsko Naselje, while number 2 is Otes, and number 3 is the Serb half of Ilidza. The Muslim half of Ilidza is -- well, do you agree that over here the Muslim parts of Ilidza are Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica? 4, 5 and 6, could you use those numbers to denote Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Again, we selected to use this block here [indicates] as Butmir. So if I put a 4 there [marks], it encompasses all that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you accept that these three neighbourhoods that we see on the map, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica, are actually on the north of this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand "north of this map."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, I meant "north" in terms of this part that is controlled by the Muslim forces that you denoted with the number 4. You see these three small concentrations or neighbourhoods. Is Butmir right by the airport runway, and then Sokolovic Kolonija, and then to the south Hrasnica, right by Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Now I understand. Yes, the figure 4 area is the northern part of that area held by the Presidency beyond the airport, which divides figures 1, figures 3, and figures 2 from 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that above Hrasnica is Mount Igman, and you tried to place your observers there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That's where Mount Igman is. Yes, we were persistent, but unsuccessful, at putting observers at Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Igman is a dominant feature, in relation to this map, and that the Muslim artillery could target any one of these points from Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, it was a significant geographical feature and, therefore, of significance militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree -- or, actually, you said that yourself, that the inaccuracy of the reports on the number of shells is partly due to the fact that there was no insight as to the outgoing fire from Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That would be part of the solution, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put the date there and your initials, and then I'm going to tender this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: [Marks]. I've forgotten the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Time flies. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as Exhibit D537.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now that we're on the subject of these statistics, let us try to clarify this discrepancy, although you have explained quite a bit of this. Can we now have 1D2216, please. It's shoot rep -- [In English] 21st of September, 1992. [Interpretation] 1D2216. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this report about the incoming and outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here one incoming round from the side of Presidency and 16 incoming to the Serbian side. It's interesting that 15 shells were registered as outgoing fire from the Serb position, and that is, in fact, what you called the restricted character of UNMO observations regarding Mount Igman. Does this corroborate what you said about that mission being fairly restricted by the lack of access to Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: You'll note, at the top of the form, that there is a qualifier. Now, that qualifier, which I'll read out: "In analysing the following information, it must be borne in mind that not all heavy weapons of either side are monitored ...," now, that caveat appears on, I think, every submission we made, because we were trying to explain to others, who were not present, the restrictions which we faced in monitoring the activities around the city. So what applied to one side applied quite equally to the other, in that we did not monitor all heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many observers would you have needed to record absolutely everything, all the incoming and all the outgoing fire in this entire zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: To answer that question, one would have to analyse the types of weapon that were employed in the conflict, assess their ranges. That would give you the geographical spread that you had to cover from the center of Sarajevo, and it would be extremely significant. It would be almost impossible to fulfill the task 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, more than 60 observers would certainly be in a better position to follow what was going on; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It certainly would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about 120, would that be enough to cover everything, Hadzici, Vogosca, Igman, and this inner city?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It's as if, in answering this question, that we're dealing in Sarajevo alone. But as we know, Sarajevo was part of a regional conflict.
