So, surely, if we draw a hypothetical circle around the center -- from the center of Sarajevo which encompasses those weapons with the greatest range, it doesn't accommodate the mobility of weapons, your ability to bring them into the zone, your ability to take them out of the zone, and it doesn't encompass any of the front-lines, because it shows no relevance to the front-lines, because you've now gone beyond Sarajevo and you've gone into the general conflict in Bosnia. So your question would ultimately be: Would we ever have enough observers for Bosnia? And, of course, the answer must be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, what is your estimate? What would be sufficient, approximately, for Sarajevo, 120, 180, or more than that, so that you could truly have proper insight into everything and there would be no discrepancies in terms of incoming and outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I think this question's now been asked twice and answered twice by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Let's move on to your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you admit this document, though?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have D509. It is 1D2138. This is after you left. It's a similar example, so let us just establish the pattern involved. So it is D509. Could we have that in e-court, please. And then could we please have page 4 out of 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I now draw your attention to 1: [In English] "Fire was observed from Serb positions: Artillery, 41; mortars, 47; tanks, 25; MRLS, 25. "The following outgoing fire was observed from the Presidency positions: Artillery, 196; mortars, 26; tank, nil; MRLS, 5; and anti-aircraft artillery, 19." [Interpretation] Now let us have a look at incoming fire: [In English] "The following incoming fire was observed on the Serb-controlled area: Artillery, 26; mortar, 124; tanks, nil; MRLS, nil; and anti-aircraft artillery, nil. Four, number 4, the following incoming fire was observed on Presidency-controlled areas: Artillery, 104; mortars, 344; and tanks, 3." [Interpretation] What can we conclude on the basis of this report, Colonel? If it will be of any assistance to you, perhaps we could say the Serbs are firing 41 shells and the Muslims over 90. And then how is it possible for the Muslims to fire 196 shells and only 26 shells fall on Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I think I've made my position very clear relating to the limited number of weapons that were monitored. I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there any way of finding out where the remaining Muslim shells are, the 170 Muslim shells that we don't know where they fell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, we see that Serbs fired 26 rounds, and 104 fell on Muslim territory. Now, who fired the difference of 78 shells that landed on Muslim territory but were not fired from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I think I can say, for probably the last time, the statistics that you see in front of you are an inexact representation. It was an attempt to indicate levels of activity. Those observations were made by UN military observers on limited number of gun sites and on a limited number of OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that we cannot draw accurate conclusions about the involvement of sides; we can only see the total number of rounds?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That's not strictly the case. I've already indicated that the Lima side, the Serb side, monitored a number of weapon sites. We know that there were other weapon sites we did not monitor. Now, the same applies to the Presidency side, not so much within Sarajevo because there was a very limited number of heavy weapons available to the Presidency side, but it certainly applied by virtue of the Presidency weapons beyond the area of immediate conflict, Sarajevo city. So the observers who were watching Sarajevo city can give an extremely good rendition of their understandings of tensions and impacts within the city, but I don't think that you can take it to a statistical conclusion, which is perhaps what your interpretation appears to be. It's about giving an overall impression of military activity within the sector.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is an exhibit, isn't it? 509 is an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to spend some time on the issue of negotiations that you were rather familiar with, as we established yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you scored considerable successes with the Serbian side? You were able to get most of what you demanded from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: If your question is, Did we achieve co-operation at the level which I negotiated with the Serb side, then the answer is yes. By the same token, I think I obtained an equal amount of success with the Presidency side. So the answer is, yes, I certainly did have success with your -- the Presidency and the Serb side in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I feel the need to determine this for sure. In your amalgamated statement, paragraph 121, you said something to the effect that the task of the UNMOs did not include investigations, in the police sense of the word, or inquiries into responsibility for certain incidents. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, but it requires a little filling out, I think. If there's an incident within an environment which is a cease-fire, then lots of resource can be applied to that incident to determine its source, its intention, and maybe the effects of the said incident. There is, I think, a common misconception that UN military observers were able to apply that forensic approach to every incident. But, of course, we've already discussed that there was no cease-fire. The level of activity, even as a background, was beyond full application of that sort of consideration. So that's what I mean by the statement, in that you could not apply to every incident the attention that you would like to by virtue of the fact that it was not a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's just see. In your statement from 1997, on pages 5 and 6 you asserted that the Serbian side, in view of the fact that it was tactically on the rise, was expected to give more in every agreement, and the Serbian military advantage was frequently interpreted as aggression, resulting in -- [In English] "... and was not appreciated outside of the UNMOs." [Interpretation] Was this correctly stated in your 1997 statement? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I've made a number of statements. I'm not sure if your interpretation of what I said is correct, because I haven't got that statement in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If it assists the witness, I believe this statement is contained in the binder he has in front of him. That might be of assistance here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you locate that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you're looking for this, let me try to help. You claimed that Serbs had abandoned their significant tactical advantage by turning over the airport, and because the Serbs were tactically on the rise, they were frequently asked to make more concessions, and their military advantage was frequently interpreted as aggression. Those are pages 5 and 6 in your 1997 statement. This was not a quotation. This is my reading of it, but that's the gist, that entering into the airport agreement, they abandoned a significant tactical advantage, and then the rest that I just said. Is that is that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I've read the statement and -- the full statement from which you've extracted that, and I stand by that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We spent some time yesterday discussing the types of war and the nature of war, and we agreed that not all wars are the same. Do you agree that the people who fought there were the same people who lived there, and you, yourself, observed that their houses were from several yards to several hundred yards behind their lines, behind their positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, it was a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in yesterday's interview, we found some common ground, some similarities, with the situation in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, we did, just with the condition that the overall level of military activity was nowhere near the -- comparable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's time to take a break. We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. I was advised that you had something to raise in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. I believe this witness is very precious to both sides, to both parties, and to the Chamber as well. His answers are easy to understand and flowing, but they do take time and it takes up my time, but I believe that still his detailed answers will provide more information to the Chamber than those of many other witnesses, because he's a good witness and he had very good insight into the situation on the ground. And, therefore, I would like to ask the Chamber to reconsider and give me at least one more session for the cross-examination of this witness, because there are many documents that this witness can confirm or reject, and there are many elements that I would like to go through in his statements. I don't think that we will get many more such witnesses, military professionals of his kind and his level. Perhaps you could give me at least one session tomorrow, and perhaps more, and if you could, it would be really of great assistance to all the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We note, Mr. Karadzic, that you will have had about two and a half hours by the end of today, so that still you will have another half an hour to complete your cross-examination in three hours, which was allowed originally by the Chamber. Given that the witness has to come back tomorrow, and considering all the circumstances, the Chamber will grant your request, but try to conclude his evidence by the end of the first session tomorrow, including the Prosecution's redirect examination. How much do you think you need for your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: At this stage, the estimate would be 10 minutes, Your Honour. That's subject to change, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate it greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I wanted to advise the Court as -- in response to a request made this morning with regard to the scheduling of -- or the availability of Mr. Suljevic. I understand that VWS was in contact with him this morning. He is available for travel as of the 26th of August and could, therefore, be available to give evidence on or from the 27th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise, Colonel, for your inconvenience. There were some matters we had to deal with in the absence of yourself. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we hearing the interpretation? Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies of the interpreter. The microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am still on the subject of our -- yesterday's interview, when we discussed various types of war, and I would like to see if there are any similarities with other wars that you are familiar with, especially the Northern Ireland conflict, where we did not see that intensity of conflict. But do you agree that there is a similarity with Bosnia and Herzegovina, inasmuch as you can't tell who is a Muslim and who is a Serb unless they're wearing the traditional costume?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The difficulty with civil war or, as we would call it, an insurgency, is that definition of one's enemy is an extremely difficult decision to make, one that you make in an instant. So to apply our own response as a military to that, we had rules of engagement which we tried to impose on all our soldiers, and it was very much dependent on strict discipline, command, and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the British Army a professional army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't find that question relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the people who fought in Bosnia and Herzegovina on all the three sides were, in fact, local residents, some of whom had served in the Yugoslav People's Army and some of them did not even have that much military experience?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, there's a considerable mixture of military experience on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that those, for instance, who managed certain military assets were able to do that because they managed such assets during their compulsory military service, not otherwise? Do you agree, in other words, that these were not professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I don't believe you ever manage military assets. You command them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not very precise. Maybe I didn't put this too clearly. But I noticed in a number of your statements that you seem to say you had many more problems at the local level - I don't mean you, personally. I mean your observers - whereas at the higher level, the level of the corps, you did manage to get whatever you wanted, mostly, whereas at the local level it was harder? That can be a yes-or-no question, can't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Not really. It involves much more than a yes-or-no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that civilians stopped you because some of their dead relatives had not been pulled out, or the commander had his own view of things, and you had to ask the corps command to intercede?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, you refer to an incident I recall well, where some of my military observers were taken hostage for a period of time in response to an individual who had, I think, if I recall correctly, seen on television the body of his cousin, I think, and was extremely upset, and his response was to take the UN military observers hostage until he had what he saw as a satisfactory outcome for that personal grief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that involved civilians, like in the cases when they wanted their relatives pulled out from behind the lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: No, that's not an expression I would use. If you are talking about mutual body exchanges, that's a different subject. We certainly did not go onto front-lines and remove bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But can we agree that the Army of Republika Srpska came into being on the 20th of May, whereas the war started on the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your point is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to go back to our conversation yesterday; namely, that the local population and the local commanders set up front-lines, that is, defence lines, for their localities long before the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was established.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Indeed. In the early days of the conflict, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in view of the fact these local commanders and local fighting men were not a professional army stationed in barracks, and drilling and training all the time, can you understand that part of their disobedience towards commanders of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps stemmed from the fact that their families lived directly behind the front-lines and these front-lines were established before the establishment of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I comprehend the statement that in the early parts of the conflict, that the engaged forces would be more irregular than they later were. If that is your question, that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the negotiations. Can we get 65 ter 10875. It could be a Prosecution exhibit. 10875. I don't know if it's an exhibit yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a monthly report covering the month of November 1992. I believe you even signed this report. You speak here about a kind of truce. Can we turn to the 7th of November, please. You say, about the 7th of November, that the Serbs insisted on a cessation of hostilities throughout Bosnia, rather than in small areas, and you say that this is understandable because these local cease-fires [in English] "would allow the Presidency to concentrate their forces in other areas." [Interpretation] "These local cease-fires would allow the Presidency to concentrate their forces in other areas." It comes before the passage which begins with: "Taking advantage ..." It's towards the bottom of this paragraph about the 7th of November. There's "Butmir, Lukavica" in upper case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure whether the witness is able to follow the document. Why don't we collapse the B/C/S so that he can read it. Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yeah, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Again, it must be concluded that although the Serb delegation are willing to go through the motions of attendance at the Mixed Military Working Group and its subcommittees, they appear to have little intention to abandoning their previously-stated position. In particular, there seems little reason to believe that the Serbs have any intention of abandoning their stated principles that they are in favour of, either complete cease-fire and demilitarisation simultaneously across BiH or none at all, especially since the demilitarisation would allow the Presidency to concentrate their forces in other areas. The viewpoint of the Serbs is understandable."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you still say this today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, I attended the Mixed Military Working Group as an observer and contributor as was necessary. I had plenty of opportunity to watch and listen to the various participants, and I applied the knowledge I gained there with that that I had from my experience on the ground in theatre in Sarajevo, and so what you see on this report is an amalgamation of all those inputs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us not call again 17030. You say, in paragraph 11, about the November cease-fire, that it was especially useful to the Muslim forces because it enabled them to rally their forces and ammunition. Was that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding should the cease-fire have been invoked. I know that nominally, it was invoked. There was a general reduction in activity throughout the sector, but it didn't last for more than two or three days and gradually built up again. Hence, one of my earlier comments that effectively there were never useful cease-fires within the city.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. This document that is on the screen, 10875, was that tendered by the Prosecution and has it been admitted already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the associated exhibits, the number of which will be announced in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, at these morning meetings, you exchanged information. Morillon provided information to you, right, and you and the other officers exchanged information concerning the previous day; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: As to General Morillon's contribution to the meetings to which you refer, no. He was the deputy commander of UNPROFOR, but the sector commander was General Razek, and General Razek and his staff ran the meeting to which you refer, and all the agencies I have already outlined attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with General Morillon's reports, or, rather, were you familiar with what had been going on during the negotiations between the parties, the negotiations in which the UN acted as an intermediary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Do you refer here to the Mixed Military Working Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. The contacts between Morillon and -- or, rather, the UN, UNPROFOR, with parties that were in conflict.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: General Morillon was sent to command UNPROFOR's operations within Bosnia. He happened to be co-located in Sarajevo. He, therefore, was not somebody I spoke to regularly, but I spoke to him frequently. But it was not as part of my natural chain of command, so it would be informal talks that I had with General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The morning briefings that you refer to, in addition to yourself, the UNHCR, the Red Cross, did UNPROFOR take part as well? Was UNPROFOR present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yeah, may I explain. You clearly don't understand. UNPROFOR provided a sector control on Sarajevo. In the PTT building, there was a sector commander. Under his command, he had three battalions, and that is what I refer to as the sector control or the sector command. That is UNPROFOR as it was represented in Sarajevo. But the UN Military Observer mission was added to the sector, but not under command of that sector. So the meetings to which you refer, of course, are UNPROFOR meetings because they are a sector commander's meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 08561. Perhaps that would be helpful. Perhaps we will be more expeditious and more precise in that way. 08561 is the 65 ter number. Yes, that's right, the 20th of November. It's a report. It has to do with meetings between Dr. Karadzic and the commander of the BH Command. Obviously, it's the same -- yes, yes, yes, right. For the interpreters, can you keep the Serbian version there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, paragraph number 3, let's have a look at that. That is on the next page. Sorry, sorry, let's look at paragraph 2, and it says here that: "Karadzic claimed UNPROFOR was passing ammunition, Nepalese and Argentineans, and rations, NATO, and helping Muslims and Croats move in UN vehicles. He quoted one example, when a bribe of allegedly 2.000 Deutchemark was paid. He said he was sure this was happening without the knowledge of the chain of command." General Morillon goes on to say that he asked that all such information be forwarded urgently to UNPROFOR so that the perpetrators would be punished. Now let us look at paragraph 3. In English, actually, we're already on that page, but could we have paragraph 3. Paragraph number 3, Karadzic is asking that UNPROFOR try to establish who is starting the exchanges of gun-fire. We don't see paragraph number 3 here: Paragraph 2 says: "Karadzic showed considerable concern about the Croatian Republic's increasingly open intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina." The Security Council seems to be taking this, and they are persistently accusing the Serbs, passing resolutions against them, and so on and so forth. Now, paragraph number 3 says that Karadzic is asking UNPROFOR to establish who started exchanges of gun-fire. And now could we have paragraph number 7. This is what it says here: "Demilitarisation of Sarajevo: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic affirmed his belief in the importance of the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. He believed it should happen in a series of small steps and he agreed to push for progress in this respect. He discussed practical ways of achieving this in considerable detail during lunch." [Interpretation] And then he says further on: [In English] "There is some evidence already of Serb heavy weapons being moved away from Sarajevo. Where to is, however, not known." [Interpretation] Do you recall this position of ours; namely, that Sarajevo should be demilitarised, and that General Morillon communicated with us and worked on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I have to make the assumption from the text I see in front of me, but I wasn't at the lunch and I certainly wasn't at that particular meeting. But from my understanding in the Mixed Military Working Group, I think in the previous submission I'd made my case very clear as to my understanding of both the Serb and the Presidency side, so I'm not sure that I see the document in front of me as being pertinent to me, unless somebody tells me different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we scroll down a bit in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you accept that this is General Morillon's report from the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I see it on the screen for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what paragraph 9 says: "Dr. Karadzic -- [In English] "... stated over lunch that the Serbs would never accept to be ruled by Muslims. Providing the Muslims gave up their claims to rule over all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they could quite happily live alongside each other, but each with their own administration and safe-guards for minorities." [Interpretation] Were you aware of that position of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: You're now talking about politics outside my immediate remit as senior military observer. My whole concentration was upon the Sarajevo area, the conflict in the Sarajevo area, humanitarian issues, military assessments, and other UN military observer tasks which I think I have submitted already. So this is, again, outside my area of knowledge and expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was discussed, then, at these morning briefings? What was it that these people could have discussed? You, yourself, on behalf of the observers, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, the Red Cross, perhaps another agency -- when you said "agency," I was thinking of news agencies, whereas you meant humanitarian agencies and the like. So what was discussed there? Were such matters ever touched upon, that is to say, things that had to do with the mediation of the UN?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Absolutely, but the levels which we're discussing these issues vary. Quite clearly, General Morillon would have a different level of discussion with people he met. So would the force commander, of course, back in Zagreb. So did politicians who visited the region. But the meetings which you're referring to is a military meeting, which is a known, accepted, and given sequence of events to command a sector of UN troops in a theatre, so the items discussed would be much more about the activities of the battalions, the activities of the UNMOs, the absorption of information from Sarajevo, the understanding of intentions, so that we could brief those people who are making the discussions to which you refer elsewhere. So I think it's a level which you're perhaps misunderstanding, that this was a sector briefing, a military sector briefing, and it was not the sort of environment where the subjects you're mentioning were discussed in detail. The immediate environment where that sort of discussion would take place would be the Mixed Military Working Group, but that was not the daily sector meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know anything about General Morillon's activities, as well as those of the mediators? Did you know anything about their negotiations with the parties? Did you express any interest, in terms of what the wishes or aspirations of the parties were, because you said that you actually looked at the kind of cease-fire they wanted? When you talked to your colleagues from UNPROFOR, did you know what the core of our conflict was and what each of the parties wanted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. There's about four questions in there. It might be worth breaking that up so it's easier for the witness to make sure he's answering a single question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, do you like the question to be asked again or you can break them down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can try and work from this script in front, if that helps. I knew of General Morillon's intentions and negotiations, but I say again "on an informal basis," because I met him frequently on an informal basis. My task was specifically Sarajevo. My title was senior military observer, Sarajevo. Of course, what happened there was affected by and similarly affected events elsewhere in Bosnia, so I've already said today you must never take Sarajevo as a separate entity. So, in answer to your other question, yes, I think we did consider, with great care, the aims and intentions of all sides within the conflict because to not do that would be to risk making serious errors with what we were trying to do. But I think what I've just said there is separate from your question pertaining to how much I knew General Morillon was discussing with other people. He would sometimes brief, of course, the sector commander. The sector commander may or may not pass on aspects of that briefing to us on a daily basis at the sector meeting to which we have referred. I hope that answers all the questions that you asked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that this is the regular form of report that General Morillon -- or, rather, UN representatives sent to their superior commands; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The report that you're -- I'm now looking at on the screen on the right, are you asking is that I know that's the regular sort of report that they sent to their superiors? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Is this customary? Is this how reports were sent? Is this one of those reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Until today, I'd not seen one. Each element of UNPROFOR at each level of command had their own responsibilities. You've seen mine. They related to situation reports, incident reports, and similar. I assimilated information, and you've seen the type of report I submitted to the chief military observer. What others did, like the sector commander, like General Morillon, I was not party to on a day-to-day basis unless they elected to brief us at the daily meeting about the content of those particular submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this Serb position stated in paragraph 9; namely, that they wanted to have their own administration and that the Muslims should have their own administration, and that no one should be ruling all of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Mole, yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, in view of the last answer given, they were following the intentions of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could direct us to the portion that the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It's line -- page 65, the question beginning line 15: "Were you aware of that position of the Serb side?" And the witness went on to state, at line 17: "You're now talking about politics outside my immediate remit as senior military observer," and goes on to explain how it is outside his remit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Precisely. Move on to your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go down a bit so that we see General Morillon's signature on the page in English. And you see what number 10 says, that the meeting was successful. Or, rather, this is a telegram. There is no signature, actually. Thank you. Can this telegram of Morillon's be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection to the authenticity of this document, and, in principle, no objection to its admission, but I don't think the witness has added anything of evidential value here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We agree with Mr. Hayden's observation. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about this document, so we'll not admit this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 08563. Perhaps he will know a bit more about the phenomena referred to in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I do believe that you did not see each and every document that we have here, but you were familiar with the phenomena that these documents relate to; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Let's look at the documents, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 1 says who was present on the Serb side. It is the military and political leadership; Karadzic, Koljevic, Mladic, Gvero and Zarkovic. As for the UNPROFOR Command, Morillon, Andreiev, Magnusson and Tucker. Have you heard of these meetings? This meeting was held on the 27th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I was aware that, as I've already stated, that meetings went on at every level of command within UNPROFOR. This is one example of said meetings. At the same time that this meeting would be occurring, there would be many others, from local UN military observers talking to the gentleman or lady who owned the house they happened to occupy, right the way through to the force commander, so this is of no surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what paragraph 3 says "Personal Assessment of Situation": [In English] "Presidency. If Dr. Karadzic wanted negotiations for peace to be successful, it would be crucial that his forces did not retaliate for the provocations which could continue for some while. Heavy retaliations would be exactly what the radical faction is trying to provoke." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this conclusion of General Morillon's?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Could you give me a moment? Perhaps it lost something in its translation from French to English, so I would like to read it again, if I might.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph A in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, I have the right paragraph. Just give me a moment, please. Yes, that would be a major concern of both sides, not just the Serb side, but Presidency too. The difficulty of extracting from a position of conflict to a temporary cease-fire or even a long-term cease-fire would be a very difficult and complex operation, one, incidentally, that we had considered the contribution of the UNMOs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that provocations and responses to provocations worked in favour of radical elements? Did you know what this radical faction was in the Presidency, the one that General Morillon was speaking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: From what I see in front of me, he has not mentioned a specific radical faction. I think it would be fair to interpret this particular paragraph equally for both sides as a difficulty of withdrawing from combat position to a position of relative quiet or cease-fire. I don't necessarily, therefore, read this paragraph as being more weighted to one side more than the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, with all due respect, Colonel, this only has to do with the Presidency, a presidency. And then the assessment of General Morillon is stated there about the positions of the Presidency, and he is advising the Serb side not to respond because that works in favour of the radicals in the Presidency. This only has to do with the Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, but it won't have escaped your notice that the meeting was between BH Command and the Bosnian Serbs. No doubt, should they have had a meeting between BH Command and the Presidency, exactly the same paragraph would have to be included.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see paragraph 5. That's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This assumption of yours may be right, and maybe not, but do you agree it is a fact that the Muslim side invested efforts in actually provoking a Serb response, which is the point of every provocation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That what you state was true, I haven't the slightest doubt. I agree with you completely. But, and there's always a "but," I have to say that in my experience, and bearing in mind that we were in a war situation, what happened on one side certainly occurred on the other as well. So I don't interpret your statement as being purely one problem that associates itself with the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at paragraph 5, point A: "Dr. Karadzic reaffirmed the right of all Serbs, Croats, and Muslims in BH to freedom, self-determination and security." [In English] "The problem lay in the lack of confidence and trust. The outsiders, it might appear that they at times did not want peace, but this was actually because they could not accept things because they did not trust each other -- the other side. He requested patience whilst trust was rebuilt at the pace of those involved in the conflict. He did, however, trust the UN." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this assessment by General Morillon, and do you agree with my assessment that the lack of trust between the parties disrupted all efforts to achieve peace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Surely, the expression that the lack of trust was a major hurdle in the creation of an atmosphere for peace is exactly that, it is the cause of war. I read the paragraph, and I nod and say to myself, That's one of the main causes of war. I don't particularly see it as a significant comment beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Just so that the record is accurate, Dr. Karadzic stated that this was an assessment of General Morillon and then talked about an assessment of his own. The document, I think, indicates that this was an assessment by Dr. Karadzic that General Morillon had noted down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That saves us time in redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what terminology Dr. Karadzic used: "Dr. Karadzic emphasised agreement to the use by the UN of the term 'cessation of hostilities' as a 'cease-fire' implied that one could regroup and resupply in preparation for starting the fighting again." Do you agree that our fear of limited cessation of hostilities was justified because the Muslim side grew from strength to strength?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: All parties to a conflict would surely take advantage of a cease-fire to reposition themselves should hostilities continue. That's a military fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in view of the situation in Sarajevo, would you agree with your own conclusion that the Serbs cared very much for maintaining the status quo? What would cease-fires give to Serbs, anyway? They had no intention, as it was, of taking Muslim parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It seems that there is an overlay that you're making here of Serb intention for a cease-fire that didn't happen. Now, I wasn't aware of all the details that related to Serb ambitions because I wasn't, obviously, part of their high command, but -- both for military or political reasons, and so many of the assessments I made were made by my own observations. So I'm not sure that I can answer your question, because I'm not actually sure that I understand the point of it. Perhaps if you could make it clear, I could try and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I seem to remember, and I remind you of your own reports in which you noted, quite correctly, I believe, that Serbs conducted a policy of containment to keep the status quo in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see paragraph 12 of this report. That's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says: "Recommendations. The Bosnian Serb authorities are, I believe, genuinely interested in progress." [In English] "It is now necessary to show some patience with their internal difficulties, to explain this to the media, and to try to influence the radical wing of the Presidency." [Interpretation] Do you agree -- do you see that General Morillon again refers to the radical wing of the Presidency that does not favour peace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, he's addressing that issue. But, of course, one must recall that he's addressing that issue to a meeting made up of a certain faction, so clearly -- and I'm interpreting this as much as you are, but I wasn't at the meeting, I would assume that he would make very similar observations, should he have the opportunity to do so, when he spoke to the Presidency side. But these aren't documents that I know of, and I certainly, necessarily, didn't know everything that General Morillon did, so the questions are one step removed from my own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think General Morillon dealt with the same incidents as you, only at a different level. Let's just turn the page and see to whom this was addressed. Turn to the first page, rather. Is it the case that the general was addressing this to the command in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, he seems to have addressed it to HQ UNPROFOR for the attention of the force commander.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I think we're in the same position as the previous document, Your Honour. No objection to the authenticity and no objection, in principle, to the admission, but the witness has stated that he is not aware of this meeting, nor document, and wasn't able to comment substantively on its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the colonel confirmed the Serbian position concerning containment in Sarajevo. He knows about these talks. Of course, he can't be familiar with every document, but he knows about the phenomenon in general, the process that was underway and that was led by General Morillon. He knows that General Morillon mediated between the sides and tried to achieve peace, and he made assessments to what extent the Serbian side was dedicated to progress. And this concerns a time when Colonel Mole was in Sarajevo. We cannot only admit the documents that a witness has personally seen. This is about the general context, about events. Are we doubting the authenticity of events or the activity of General Morillon there at the time, things that the colonel was familiar with? On page 72 and 73, he did -- he did confirm some passages, Colonel Mole did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may remind you, my adversary is tendering a lot of associated documents. This particular document can be confirmed, in terms of authenticity, by the witness. The other side is tendering a lot of related documents. I believe this one should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unlike the previous document, Colonel Mole confirmed some situation, for example, which is related to para 3. So on that basis, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have two minutes, Mr. Karadzic, for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to take advantage of the fact that in the last paragraph, General Morillon mentioned that it would be a good thing to demonstrate some patience and to suggest to the media that they should have some understanding for the Serbian side. And I see that you, too, were very critical of the media and their reporting. I see, in your amalgamated statement, paragraph 134, relates to the not-always-accurate reporting by the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, I feel very strongly about the interpretation of events, as I saw them, from a position of comparative strengths, I think, by virtue of the officers who worked for me, the knowledge I was able to gather, and the military and civil interpretation that I applied was based on good evidence. I was always concerned that the evidence base that was used by certain agencies, and in this regard I refer to news agencies, was extremely weak. I am, in my own mind, convinced that there was a considerable anti-Serb approach to the conflict within the press and, indeed, beyond it to some quite senior politicians who I met and talked with in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be it for today, and we'll continue tomorrow. Colonel Mole, I thought that we would be able to conclude your evidence today, but unfortunately we can't. I believe that your evidence could be concluded by the first session tomorrow, i.e., by 10.20 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I believe that you know well, but in the meantime you're not supposed to discuss with anybody about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll rise today, and we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
